hooks.text: A tiny particle hit Earth with the force of a fast-pitched baseball.
One single proton carried 47,000,000 times the energy of our best colliders.
The fastest visitor to Earth was invisible and hit like a professional athlete.

title: The Invisible Particle With the Energy of a Baseball
description: The Oh-My-God particle hit Earth in 1991 with 47 million times the energy of our best accelerators, yet its source remains a complete mystery.

beats.text: A tiny particle hit Earth with the force of a fast-pitched baseball.
beats.visual: artist's concept of a high-energy cosmic ray air shower hitting Earth's atmosphere

beats.text: In October 1991, the Fly’s Eye detector in Utah caught a visitor traveling at nearly light speed.
beats.visual: photograph of the Fly's Eye detector array at Dugway Proving Ground, Utah

beats.text: Dubbed the Oh-My-God particle, it packed 320 exaelectronvolts of kinetic energy.
beats.visual: diagram of an extensive air shower collision in Earth's atmosphere

beats.text: That is 47,000,000 times more energy than any machine humans have ever built.
beats.visual: photograph of the Large Hadron Collider tunnel at CERN

beats.text: Most assume such power requires a massive engine, like the jets of a supermassive black hole.
beats.visual: artist's concept of an active galactic nucleus with powerful jets

beats.text: But tracing its arrival path back reveals absolutely nothing in the darkness where it began.
beats.visual: astronomical deep field image showing the region of the Oh-My-God particle's origin

beats.text: In 2021, the Amaterasu particle arrived from an even emptier cosmic void.
beats.visual: photograph of a scintillator at the Telescope Array project in Utah

beats.text: These cosmic voids keep firing mysteries just like this:
beats.visual: artist's concept of a subatomic particle shower hitting Earth at night
